evidence.claim: Follow the Bear River through a mountain pass toward Umbagog Lake.
evidence.quote: travels along Route 26 to Grafton Notch State Park and Lake Umbagog

evidence.claim: Follow the Bear River
evidence.quote: This byway follows along the Bear River for much of the trip.

evidence.claim: through a mountain pass
evidence.quote: surrounding Grafton Notch, the mountain pass between Old Speck Mountain and Baldpate Mountain

evidence.claim: Grafton Notch Scenic Byway follows rural, two-lane Route 26 beside the Bear River for much of its journey.
evidence.quote: This byway follows along the Bear River for much of the trip. Journeying along this rural two-lane road

evidence.claim: The National Scenic Byway Foundation identifies it as a 21-mile state byway and highlights a landscape of old farmhouses, stone walls, state parkland and working forest.
evidence.quote: Details Designation State Byway Location ME Length 21 miles

evidence.claim: The pass lies between Old Speck and Baldpate in the Mahoosuc Range.
evidence.quote: the mountain pass between Old Speck Mountain and Baldpate Mountain, mountains in the Mahoosuc Range.

evidence.claim: The road through Newry belonged to a longer trade connection: the Portland-to-Errol route, completed in 1802, followed what is now Route 26.
evidence.quote: The trade route (now Route 26) from Portland to Errol, New Hampshire, completed in 1802, passed through Newry.

evidence.claim: Farms occupied the intervales, hay became the principal crop, and the Bear River supported a sawmill and gristmill.
evidence.quote: Farms were established on the intervales, which had excellent soil. Hay was the principal crop. Slopes of the mountains provided pasturage for grazing animals. A sawmill and gristmill were built on the Bear River

evidence.claim: A different land use took shape in 1963, when Maine bought 2,875 acres from Brown Company for the state park; further purchases fixed its boundaries in 1977.
evidence.quote: In 1963, the state made its first acquisitions of the land for the park with the purchase of 2,875 acres (1,163 ha) from Brown Company. The addition of 18 more parcels, many less than 5 acres, took place in the 1960s, mostly in 1964. The park boundaries were fixed with the addition of two one-acre parcels in 1977.

evidence.claim: Begin in Newry, north of Sunday River Ski Area, and follow Route 26 toward Grafton Notch State Park.
evidence.quote: The Grafton Notch scenic byway begins in Newry, just north of the Sunday River Ski Area, and travels along Route 26 to Grafton Notch State Park

evidence.claim: Screw Auger Falls occupies a steep gorge along the Bear River.
evidence.quote: Screw Auger Falls is located within a steep gorge along the Bear River

evidence.claim: Beyond the notch, the byway continues toward Lake Umbagog on the New Hampshire border.
evidence.quote: travels along Route 26 to Grafton Notch State Park and Lake Umbagog, which crosses the New Hampshire border.

evidence.claim: highlights a landscape of old farmhouses, stone walls, state parkland and working forest.
evidence.quote: Old farmhouses and weathered stone walls mark the landscape, much of which is now either a designated state park or privately-owned working forestland.

evidence.claim: The Bear River once supplied Newry with more than a route through the mountains: a sawmill and gristmill were built on its banks.
evidence.quote: A sawmill and gristmill were built on the Bear River

evidence.claim: Farms occupied the intervales, where the soil favored agriculture, while mountain slopes supplied grazing land.
evidence.quote: Farms were established on the intervales, which had excellent soil. Hay was the principal crop. Slopes of the mountains provided pasturage for grazing animals.

evidence.claim: Hay was the principal crop.
evidence.quote: Hay was the principal crop.

evidence.claim: The trade road from Portland to Errol passed through town in 1802, along the route now numbered 26.
evidence.quote: The trade route (now Route 26) from Portland to Errol, New Hampshire, completed in 1802, passed through Newry.

evidence.claim: Newry is now home to Sunday River Ski Resort, with a large seasonal winter population alongside its year-round residents.
evidence.quote: The town is best known as the home of Sunday River Ski Resort and has a proportionately large seasonal (winter) population.

evidence.claim: At Screw Auger Falls, the Bear River occupies a steep gorge in Grafton Notch State Park.
evidence.quote: Screw Auger Falls is located within a steep gorge along the Bear River

evidence.claim: When water levels are low enough, boulders left by glacial processes are visible in the stream.
evidence.quote: when water levels are low enough, erratics are visible in the stream.

evidence.claim: The notch preserves U-shaped valleys and rock exposed by erosion, including Devonian granite cut by pegmatite intrusions.
evidence.quote: Notable geomorphology of the park includes U-shaped valleys, gorges, and esker. Erosional processes expose the unique bedrock composed of Devonian granite with pegmatite intrusions.

evidence.claim: The precise origin of the gorges remains debated: meltwater could have carved them during the ice sheet’s retreat or beneath the ice under high pressure.
evidence.quote: responsibility for gorge formation is debated; "they may have formed while the ice sheet retreated north of the region and contributed a large quantity of meltwater, or more likely, they formed while the ice sheet covered the area and the subglacial water was under very high pressure".

evidence.claim: At low water, boulders left by glacial processes are visible in the Bear River gorge.
evidence.quote: when water levels are low enough, erratics are visible in the stream.

evidence.claim: Umbagog straddles Maine and New Hampshire, with an average depth of 10 feet.
evidence.quote: Its average depth is 10 feet (3.0 m)

evidence.claim: Its name is said to come from the Abenaki word for shallow water.
evidence.quote: is said to come from the Abenaki word for "shallow water"

evidence.claim: The lake has changed: construction of a dam at Errol in the 19th century markedly increased both its area and depth.
evidence.quote: The lake's area and depth were markedly increased with the construction of a dam at Errol in the 19th century.

evidence.claim: The Magalloway, Rapid and Dead Cambridge rivers feed it, and the Androscoggin flows from it.
evidence.quote: Umbagog Lake is fed by the Magalloway River, the Rapid River, and the Dead Cambridge River. It is the source of the Androscoggin River.

evidence.claim: Along the northwest shore, a natural floating island consists of generations of decomposing marsh vegetation.
evidence.quote: An interesting feature along its northwest shore is an expansive natural floating island composed of generations of decomposing marshland vegetation.

evidence.claim: Umbagog straddles Maine and New Hampshire
evidence.quote: Umbagog Lake is a wilderness lake located in Coös County, New Hampshire, and Oxford County, Maine.

evidence.claim: Glaciation left U-shaped valleys and scattered boulders across the valley floor; erosion exposes granite in the park’s gorges.
evidence.quote: Additionally, these processes scattered erratics over the u-shaped valley floor.

evidence.claim: Glaciation left U-shaped valleys
evidence.quote: Grafton Notch reflects the glaciation processes carved by the Laurentide Ice sheet during the Wisconsin Glaciation episode. Notable geomorphology of the park includes U-shaped valleys, gorges, and esker.

evidence.claim: erosion exposes granite in the park’s gorges.
evidence.quote: Erosional processes expose the unique bedrock composed of Devonian granite with pegmatite intrusions.

evidence.claim: The Bear River rises in the notch and flows southeast to the Androscoggin; Route 26 follows its entire course.
evidence.quote: It rises in Grafton Notch at the northeastern end of the Mahoosuc Range and flows southeast, joining the Androscoggin in the town of Newry.  Maine Route 26 follows the entire course of the river.

evidence.claim: Both the Bear River and Sunday River drain the town and flow into the Androscoggin.
evidence.quote: Newry is drained by the Bear River and Sunday River, which both flow into the Androscoggin River.

evidence.claim: Visible pegmatite veins cross the gorges’ water-eroded bedrock, another detail of the exposed rock alongside the valley’s larger glacial forms.
evidence.quote: Many pegmatite vein intrusions are visible around the water-eroded bedrock of the gorges.

evidence.claim: The lake covers 7,850 acres and reaches a maximum depth of 45 feet below its surface.
evidence.quote: Its surface area is 7,850 acres (31.8 km2)

evidence.claim: a maximum depth of 45 feet
evidence.quote: its maximum depth is 45 feet (14 m).

flags: Cache gives no byway designation date, campaign history, driving time or detailed grades; the road history uses the documented 1802 trade route and later park acquisition without equating their dates with scenic designation.
Material strip mileage runs opposite the cached byway description. Moments follow the documented Newry-to-Umbagog direction; Umbagog remains a separate excursion.
Gorge formation is disputed in the cache; no single glacial mechanism is asserted.
Umbagog name derivation retains the source’s qualification; no Abenaki community source is cached.
Intro describes terrain and the two-lane river road; no sourced curves, grades or travel time are available. Newry is added as the third moment without displacing either published landmark.
